To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the invasive migration of neoplastically transformed cells is based on the development of distinct phenotypes, each being characterized by a particular pattern of cytoskeletal reorganizations.

the invasive phenotype of neoplastic epithelial cells is based on a decrease of contractility, which results in a loss of adhesion, and an increase of motility, which is due to a loss of polarity and a loss of the ability to maintain the shape of a polarized cell.

RhoA is a key regulator of cell contractility, that RhoA activity is regulated by the activity of the GTPase-activating protein p190RhoGAP, and that p190Rho-GAP is a target of the Ras-RalGDS signaling pathway.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the genes responsible for the invasive phenotype, and with the elucidation of their molecular interactions.

the elucidation of the molecular mechanisms of invasive migration of transformed neoplastic and of normal cells, and of the molecular mechanisms responsible for the development of the malignant phenotype.
the identification of the mechanisms of invasive behavior of neoplastic cell populations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

neoplastic cells are able to invade tissues because they are capable of undergoing Rho-dependent alterations of contractility and because they express genes for adhesive structures which enable them to adhere to and to invade tissues.
neoplastic transformation is not a single event, but a complex of events, each of which may be responsible for one of the many aspects of the invasive phenotype.
the cytoskeleton is the main target of the genetic events responsible for the development of invasive phenotypes in neoplastic cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the development of the invasive phenotype is based on the interplay of two distinct genetic programs: one responsible for alterations in contractility and the other for changes in adhesiveness.
the Rho-dependent contractile apparatus and the adhesive structures are the major targets of genetic alterations in invasive neoplastic cells.
Rho is a key player in cytoskeletal mechanisms which control the invasive phenotype of neoplastic cell populations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
invasive phenotypes of neoplastic epithelial cells are determined by the interplay of contractility and cell adhesion.

invasive phenotypes can be generated by a variety of mechanisms and that the mechanisms of invasive migration of neoplasm cells are not necessarily identical to the mechanisms of normal epithelio-mechanical transformations.
the cytoskeleton of invasive cells is not just a passive structure, but an active one, which can be used to generate contractile tension.
